title: Quadratic Sample Complexity for Strictly Replicable Realizable Learning with Unknown Marginals
summary: Under the quantifier $\exists A\,\forall D$, where the realizable distribution and its marginal are unknown, we determine the finite-class sample-complexity exponent for strict replicability: two independent samples and one shared seed must produce identical functions. For $\varepsilon=δ=ρ=10^{-4}$, the worst case over $|H|\le M$ is $Θ((\log M)^2)$, without iterated logarithms. For $d\ge1$, $0<\varepsilon\le1/16$, and $0<δ,ρ\le10^{-3}$, every randomized, possibly improper learner valid throughout an explicit anchored realizable family requires $Ω(d^2/(\varepsilonρ^2))$ samples. For the full Boolean class $P_d$, $d\ge2$, in the same parameter range, we prove the matching characterization $Θ(d^2/(\varepsilonρ^2)+\varepsilon^{-1}\log(1/δ))$ using a proper Poissonized ball-sampling algorithm. We also give an explicit proper Gibbs upper bound for every finite measurable Boolean class. Our lower bound uses square-root probabilities and volumetric packing; the Gibbs proof builds on established coupling and generalization identities. Finally, we characterize the known-marginal worst case for $P_d$, showing why that interface must be kept distinct.

title: Dynamic Dual-Feedback Conformal Inference for Time Series Forecasting
summary: Quantifying uncertainty in time series forecasting is particularly demanding because sequential data exhibit temporal dependence and are prone to distributional changes. Conformal inference has emerged as a powerful uncertainty quantification approach through the construction of prediction sets. Recent advances have introduced online conformal methods that adaptively adjust prediction thresholds through feedback mechanisms. However, the existing feedback mechanism typically relies solely on miscoverage indicators (actual feedback), whether the true label falls within the interval at each time step, while overlooking the empirical prediction threshold (estimated feedback) that is derived from the oracle conformal method. In this paper, we propose Dynamic Dual-feedback Conformal Inference (DDCI), which incorporates a dual-feedback mechanism consisting of actual feedback and estimated feedback. The former drives the primary adjustment of the intervals based on true observations, while the latter dampens excessive expansions or contractions by leveraging empirical thresholds from conformal inference during updates. By balancing these two signals, DDCI achieves more stable and narrower prediction intervals in sequential settings while maintaining near-nominal coverage in practice.

title: Robust Latent Variable Graphical Models: Exact Recovery and Fundamental Limits
summary: We study robust estimation of a Gaussian precision matrix that decomposes as a sparse matrix minus a symmetric, possibly indefinite, low-rank matrix, a structure that arises when latent-variable marginalization is combined with conditioning on linear measurements. The proposed convex estimator replaces the sample covariance by the centered Gaussian measure-transformed (MT) covariance, which preserves the signed graph of the sparse component under the nominal model, and penalizes the low-rank component by the nuclear norm of a congruence transform, an atomic norm that encodes structural side information. Our main result is a primal--dual witness theorem: under restricted invertibility and irrepresentability conditions on the Fisher information, the raw convex optimizer is unique, has no false edges, recovers the signs of all sufficiently strong edges, and has exactly the true rank and inertia. These conditions reduce to the graphical-lasso conditions when the low-rank part is absent, and we verify them from primitive incoherence and near-isotropy assumptions. Over a class on which they hold uniformly, we prove information-theoretic limits for Frobenius estimation, signed graph recovery, and inertia recovery. In particular, inertia recovery requires $N\gtrsim p/ν_{\min}^2$ samples, where $ν_{\min}$ is the smallest nonzero eigenvalue modulus of the low-rank part; the spectral beta-min condition of the witness theorem is necessary up to a $\sqrt{\log p}$ factor; and the Frobenius risk attains the minimax rate up to a factor $\sqrt{μ(1+\min\{d,r\})\log p}$, where $μ$ is the incoherence parameter, $d$ the maximal degree, and $r$ the rank. We further quantify robustness under Huber contamination, with a bias bound that is sharp for the MT functional and vanishes for remote outliers, and give a globally convergent linearized ADMM with closed-form updates.

title: Gaussian Approximation of Besov Functions for Logistic Classification on Manifolds
summary: We study Gaussian kernel approximation and regularized logistic classification on a connected compact smooth embedded manifold $X\subset\mathbb R^d$ without boundary and of intrinsic dimension $\varrho$. Two main challenges are to derive a fast oracle inequality without assuming a bounded Bayes function and to construct Gaussian approximants that exploit both the intrinsic dimension and the target's regularity without saturation. We address the first challenge through a Bernstein-type inequality whose constant depends linearly on the supremum norm of the predictor. Combined with localized complexity estimates, this yields an oracle inequality over separable normed function spaces. To address the second challenge, we establish a uniform Sobolev operator expansion and cancel its lower-order bias terms using a signed combination of Gaussian kernel integral operators at different bandwidths. Real interpolation then gives an $L_2(X)$ approximation error of order $γ^α$ for functions in $B^α_{2,\infty}(X)$, where $γ$ is the bandwidth. By constructing the approximants directly on the manifold without ambient extension, we obtain a squared Gaussian RKHS norm bound of order $γ^{-\varrho}$. This construction thus overcomes second-order saturation while retaining norm control governed by the intrinsic dimension. When the marginal distribution has a density $g\in L_p(X)$, these results yield the logistic excess-risk rate $\bigl((\log n)^{\varrho+1}/n\bigr)^{4α(1-1/p)/(4α(1-1/p)+3\varrho)}$. We further show that clipping predictions yields the faster clipped logistic excess-risk rate $\bigl((\log n)^{\varrho+2}/n\bigr)^{2α(1-1/p)/(2α(1-1/p)+\varrho)}$. For bounded densities, its polynomial exponent matches that of the minimax optimal rate for squared-loss regression, and its corresponding excess misclassification risk also matches the minimax optimal rate.

title: On the Accuracy of Approximate Leave-One-Out with Blockwise Nonsmooth Regularization in High-dimensions
summary:
Approximate leave-one-out (ALO) refers to methods that provide computationally efficient and statistically accurate approximations to leave-one-out risk estimation. These methods have recently attracted increased attention because of their connections to other important problems, including machine unlearning and data valuation. For empirical risk minimization, ALO methods often rely on a few Newton steps and therefore require smooth loss functions and regularizers. In high-dimensional problems, however, regularizers are frequently non-smooth. This has motivated the development of heuristic ALO methods for non-smooth regularization, whose empirical accuracy is often strong but whose theoretical justification remains limited.
  In this paper, we study the accuracy of a heuristic ALO method for a broad class of non-differentiable penalties that promote block sparsity in the proportional high-dimensional regime. Assuming uniformly bounded block sizes, we prove that the expected average absolute discrepancy between the exact leave-one-out loss and its ALO approximation is $O(\log^{3/2}(en)/\sqrt{n})$. Our proof technique differs substantially from existing approaches and relies on obtaining sharp bounds on the number of active groups whose status changes between the full-data and leave-one-out estimators. In addition to yielding stronger guarantees under weaker assumptions than prior work, our analysis provides new insight into the stability of sparse estimators under perturbations of the training data.

title: Visualizing Joint Ranking Distributions in Network Meta-Analysis with Hammock Plots
summary: Treatment ranking provides a summary of the relative effectiveness of competing treatments and is a key output of network meta-analysis (NMA). Existing visualizations primarily summarize marginal ranking distributions or present individual treatment hierarchies with limited insight into uncertainty in the overall hierarchy. We introduce hammock plots as a visualization framework for the joint posterior distribution of treatment rankings. Although motivated by treatment ranking in NMA, the proposed framework is broadly applicable to any setting in which uncertainty in posterior rankings is of interest. Specifically, we develop separate hammock plots to display relationships between (a) adjacent treatments or (b) adjacent ranks. Using highlighting, we show how to assess posterior support for selected treatment hierarchies, to evaluate hierarchies identified by ranking metrics against the posterior distribution, and to examine uncertainty within selected regions of the treatment hierarchy. We apply the proposed visualizations to a thrombolytic treatment network, which revealed patterns in the posterior ranking distribution and the location of uncertainty in treatment hierarchies that were difficult to identify using existing ranking graphics. We also provide a web application to generate all of the proposed hammock plot variations for any data set.

title: Choose your own adventure: How data source selection shapes urban accessibility analyses
summary: Urban park accessibility shapes mental health, physical well-being, and community cohesion. Measuring it is thus central to urban and landscape planning. Although researchers have debated the impacts of different accessibility measures on analysis results, scant attention has been paid to variability from data source selection. Do the results of accessibility analyses vary depending on the dataset used to define park locations and attributes? We compare four widely used geospatial data sources - OpenStreetMap, Esri, SafeGraph, and The Trust for Public Land - by validating their data and measuring park access across two cities. These datasets purport to cover the same spatial features, but our findings reveal wide discrepancies in accessibility results, driven by differences in dataset completeness, coverage, and accuracy between the sources. We provide guidelines for selecting and carefully validating data for accessibility analyses, as these decisions directly impact the accuracy and equity of downstream urban park planning and decision-making.

title: A parametric mixture cure rate model with competing risks
summary: The well-known standard mixture cure model is widely used to model long-term survivors by distinguishing cured from non-cured individuals in the study population. Since its seminal introduction by Berkson and Gage, numerous extensions have been proposed to enhance its flexibility and applicability across diverse clinical settings. However, most existing extensions focus on a single cause of failure among non-cured individuals, often treating events from alternative causes as censored observations. This limitation may inadequately represent the complexity of survival data in which individuals are exposed to multiple competing causes of failure. In particular, treating competing events as non-informative censoring when estimating the probability of a specific cause of failure may lead to biased estimates of cumulative incidence and potentially misleading clinical interpretations. These limitations motivate the development of flexible survival models that jointly account for long-term survivors and multiple competing causes of failure. In this study, we propose an extension of the standard mixture cure model that incorporates a cure fraction and multiple competing risks within a unified framework. Model parameters are estimated by maximum likelihood using augmented data. The finite-sample performance of the proposed estimators is evaluated through extensive simulation studies, which yield satisfactory results across the scenarios considered. Finally, the proposed methodology is illustrated using melanoma patient data from the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) database, which include long-term survivors and multiple competing causes of death.

title: Diffusion Score Estimation with Shallow Neural Networks: Regularity, Approximation, and Finite-Sample Rates
summary: We study the sample complexity of estimating Ornstein--Uhlenbeck diffusion scores in $\mathbb R^d$ using denoising score matching (DSM) with finite-width shallow ReLU networks, and its implications for reverse-process sampling. Under weak differentiability and polynomial-growth conditions on normalized derivatives of the initial density, we combine complementary estimates from the Gaussian transition kernel and the initial density to obtain explicit Sobolev bounds that are uniform in time on each fixed ball. Combining these bounds with existing shallow-network approximation theory gives explicit control of the approximation error and a sufficient path-norm budget. We then use truncation and localized Rademacher complexity to establish high-probability risk bounds for path-norm-constrained empirical DSM minimizers with unbounded inputs and labels. Under additional bounded-density and sub-Gaussian assumptions, suitable choices of network width and path-norm budget yield squared $L^2(P_t)$ score risk $\widetilde O(n^{-(d+3)/(2d+3)})$ at each fixed time $t>0$, where $n$ is the number of independent training samples and $P_t$ is the forward marginal. The nonasymptotic bounds retain explicit dependence on diffusion time and the regularity and tail parameters of the initial distribution. Aggregating the score errors over a time grid and applying existing sampling theory together with an early-stopping bound yields a high-probability total-variation error $\widetilde O(n^{-(d+3)/(4d+6)})$ between the generated and original data distributions under suitable sampling parameters. Here $\widetilde O$ suppresses logarithmic factors for fixed dimension, confidence level, and initial distribution.

title: Cramer-Rao Type Bounds for Generalized Exponential Families
summary: It is well known that the sufficient statistics of an exponential family attain the usual Cramer-Rao Lower Bound (CRLB) for their expected value. In this paper, we extend this result to a broader family of distributions that includes exponential families and power-law families, with Student t-distributions as special case. To derive the generalized Cramer-Rao inequality, we first apply Eguchi's theory to Bregman divergence to obtain a Riemannian metric and then follow the approach of Amari and Nagaoka. Since this approach applies only to models with finite support, we use Cauchy-Schwarz inequality to extend it to models with countably infinite or continuous support. The resulting generalized CRLB provides a finite-sample lower bound related to the asymptotic covariance matrix of the Minimum Bregman Divergence Estimator (MBDE). We show that the sufficient statistic of the generalized family attains the generalized CRLB. Moreover, although the generalized CRLB does not, in general, coincide with the asymptotic covariance matrix of the MBDE, the covariance matrix of an estimator attaining the generalized CRLB coincides with the corresponding matrix for the joint distribution of the sample.

title: Beyond exponential tilting: sharp asymptotics and improved importance sampling for rare events
summary: A classical approach for importance sampling (IS) of a rare event is to tilt the measure using its large deviation minimizer, thereby shifting the proposal mean towards the event set. While this tilt is log-efficient, we show that the coefficient of variation of the resulting estimator still grows like $\varepsilon^{-1/4}$ in the small-noise limit $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. Motivated by sharp large deviation asymptotics and the local geometry of the event set at the minimizer, we propose improvements using a control variate or an anisotropic, non-Gaussian proposal. We prove, up to truncations that hold with high probability, and confirm empirically in high-dimensional examples, that the former bounds the coefficient of variation and the latter makes it vanish, so that a bounded number of samples suffices. Our analysis addresses both the coefficient of variation of the different proposals and their necessary and sufficient sample size based on the Kullback--Leibler divergence of the IS target from the proposal; both yield the same rates in $\varepsilon$. We demonstrate the resulting samplers, including a variant that blends the classical and the new proposal across noise levels, for a stochastic Korteweg--de Vries equation with thousands of random inputs.

title: Let Them Peek: Group Sequential Designs for A/B Testing
summary:
Randomized controlled trials, commonly known as A/B tests, are the standard mechanism for inferring causal effects of product innovations. Standard platforms evaluate these tests with fixed-horizon procedures that control the false positive rate at a predetermined time, forcing teams to wait until the end even when early data strongly indicates success or failure. Unfortunately, continuous monitoring ("peeking") invalidates these guarantees, while always-valid inference is overly conservative under a strict deadline, and group sequential designs (GSD) have received limited traction in large-scale experimentation due to operational barriers: terminal-rule preservation, autocorrelation, latent effect-size distributions, calendar-duration optimization.
  We fill in this gap by proposing a Predictive Probability of Success (PPoS) group sequential framework that is autocorrelation-aware and duration-optimal while preserving the platform's fixed-horizon terminal rule. Our key insight is that PPoS thresholds map to closed-form lift boundaries that converge to the standard test at the horizon by construction, admit an effective-sample-size correction estimated from historical A/A tests, and suffice to attain the likelihood-ratio efficiency floor.
  Experimentally on online A/A and A/B experiments, we show that the proposed policy reduces expected duration by 43.1% (7.97 days vs. 14-day baseline), increasing effective platform capacity by 76%, while retaining the guarantees on FPR and power.

title: Modular Bayesian Inference for Partially Misspecified Mixtures with Uncertain Class Labels
summary: Scientific inference often involves observations from multiple latent populations whose class memberships are uncertain and must be inferred from available data. While full Bayesian mixture modelling provides a principled approach to joint uncertainty quantification in this setting, often the model is misspecified or less trustworthy for populations that are not the target of the inference, which can distort posterior inference for the parameters of interest. We propose a modular Bayesian framework that safeguards against such biases. We decouple classification from downstream inference using fixed class probabilities, for example from a classifier trained on a subset of labelled data. We then protect inference on the parameters of interest by preventing the likelihood contributions of less trustworthy populations from influencing them. A key benefit of this principled modularization is that it greatly simplifies inference, reducing a fully joint mixture analysis to sampling label allocations, fitting the protected downstream model for each sample, and averaging the resulting posteriors. We establish calibration conditions on these class probabilities under which the proposed procedure preserves the inferential target of the analysis with known labels, and demonstrate the method in synthetic experiments and in cosmological analysis of photometric supernova samples.

title: Communication Complexity of Universal Features
summary: Motivated by the notion of features from machine learning, we study the complexity of representing data that allows for evaluation with a given family of functions. Concretely, we consider a deterministic encoder that observes $X\sim D$ and produces a finite encoding before a task $f\in\mathcal{F}\subseteq\{0,1\}^{\mathcal{X}}$ is specified. For each task, a decoder must predict $f(X)$ with error at most $\varepsilon$ under $D$. We construct an encoder that outputs a representation with $O(d^{*}\log(1/\varepsilon))$ bits, where $d^{*}$ is the dual VC dimension of $\mathcal{F}$. Our encoder greedily selects $O((d^{*}/\varepsilon)\log(1/\varepsilon))$ functions from the class and uses their joint label pattern to produce the encoding. The key idea in our upper bound is a novel potential function argument, where we compare the entropy gained from each greedy selection with the number of patterns allowed by the dual VC dimension. We present lower bounds showing that the representation length achieved by our encoder is worst-case optimal for every $d^* \ge 1$ and $\varepsilon < 1/4$ up to a universal constant factor, and instance-wise optimal for every family $\mathcal{F}$ up to an $O(\log(1/\varepsilon))$ factor. We give two ways to learn the representation from unlabeled samples, with different guarantees on the representation size and sample complexity. Experimentally, we verify the greedy construction's accuracy-size tradeoff and explore its connection to neural sparse autoencoders.

title: Control variates for dry friction under colored noise: variance rates for non-smooth observables
summary:
A control variate method was introduced by Garnier and Mertz (2022) for multivalued stochastic differential equations driven by colored noise. For smooth observables, the asymptotic variance is $O(\varepsilon^{2})$, where $\varepsilon^{2}$ is the correlation time of the noise. However, for non-smooth reliability observables, such as threshold indicators and overshoot severities, rate estimates have not been established in general.
  In this paper, rate estimates are derived for the inertial dry-friction inclusion driven by colored noise in the three regimes whose white-noise propagators are known. The asymptotic variance of the resulting control variate estimators is $O(\varepsilon^{2α})$ for $α$-Hölder observables with $α\in(0,1]$, $O(\varepsilon)$ for observables of bounded variation satisfying a one-sided continuity condition, $O(\varepsilon^{1+α})$ for observables that are both $α$-Hölder and of bounded variation, and $O(\varepsilon^{\min\{2,1+2α\}})$ for observables with finitely many $α$-cusps, where $α\in (0, 1]$ is the cusp exponent. The last three bounds hold up to logarithmic factors. Bounds on the bias of the white-noise approximation and non-asymptotic sample-size estimates are also derived, and the comparison principle is shown to be preserved under coupled time discretization. Numerical experiments in the three regimes support the predicted rates.

title: Geometry-informed importance sampling for rare events
summary: We propose GeoIS, a new importance sampling method for estimating rare event probabilities for an underlying Gaussian distribution that exploits asymptotic theory and local event geometry. The proposal distribution is a mixture of two components. The first component draws a Gaussian along the boundary near the instanton and adds to it an exponentially distributed shift into the rare event. This component is derived from the known asymptotic approximation to the optimal zero-variance proposal distribution. The second mixture component is designed to cover missing event mass due to boundary-approximation mismatch, thereby preserving unbiasedness. We rigorously analyze this sampling strategy's performance as a function of event geometry, dimension, rarity level, and number $N$ of importance samples. Under explicit and relatively mild conditions on the former three features, we prove that the squared relative error of GeoIS is bounded by $c/N$ with high probability, for an absolute constant $c$. We implement our method numerically in several examples, including a diffusion PDE problem. The numerical experiments exhibit the qualitative dependence on geometry, dimension, rarity and sample size predicted by the theory, and show that GeoIS markedly outperforms importance sampling methods that use a fully Gaussian proposal distribution.

title: Quantifying the Threat: A Bayesian Probabilistic Framework for Heavy Metal Health Risks among Children in the Densu Basin, Ghana
comment: 59 pages, 7 figures, manuscript under peer review at Stochastic Environmental Research and Risk Assessment (SERRA)
summary: Groundwater in Ghana's Densu River Basin remains a key domestic water source, but multi-metal contamination threatens children's health. Previous deterministic hazard index assessments provide limited treatment of uncertainty, co-exposure, and spatial variability. This study applies a Bayesian probabilistic framework for non-carcinogenic risk assessment using 94 groundwater samples and measurements of Fe, Mn, Ni, Pb, Cd, and As. A Bayesian regression model propagates parameter uncertainty and accounts for contaminant co-occurrence. Adaptive Hamiltonian Monte Carlo is used for posterior inference, while inverse distance weighting generates spatially continuous risk surfaces. Pb, As, and Cd dominate cumulative risk. Posterior predictive results indicate that approximately 31% of sampling sites have a probability greater than 0.5 of exceeding a hazard index (HI) of 1. The risk surface is highly heterogeneous, with a posterior mean of 0.372 and a standard deviation of 0.416. High-risk zones often reflect moderate co-exposure rather than extreme contamination by a single metal. The framework provides uncertainty-aware, spatially explicit information to support groundwater monitoring, risk mitigation, and public health planning in data-limited regions.

title: Positive, monotone, and convex Gaussian process regression with Laplacian eigenfunctions
summary: We study how to condition an existing Hilbert space Gaussian process (HSGP) expansion on positivity, monotonicity, or convexity throughout an interval. The expansion has Gaussian coefficients whose variances are given by the kernel's spectral density. At fixed covariance and noise parameters, we retain this coefficient law and represent each complete interval event as a threshold on one coefficient. Integrating out that coefficient gives a strongly log-concave marginal posterior with a normal survival weight, while conditional truncated normal sampling recovers the full constrained law. The construction also covers joint restrictions within the finite expansion. For individual restrictions, we characterize the thresholds through polynomial equations and bound posterior error from conservative numerical evaluation in total variation. Under spectral regularity, the conditioned finite posteriors converge in quadratic Wasserstein distance to the corresponding conditioned underlying GP posteriors as the computational interval expands and higher frequencies are retained. This convergence controls uniform discrepancies in the response and derivatives through the constrained order. Mercury lidar and leaf light-response applications illustrate the consequences for derivative inference.

title: Beyond Scalar Leaderboards: Adaptive Sampling for Pareto Frontier Identification in Multi-Objective LLM Arenas
summary: The evaluation of large language models (LLMs) is inherently multi-objective, as different models may offer different tradeoffs across performance dimensions such as math, code, and writing. Because such evaluations are often based on costly and time-consuming human feedback, it is important to draw reliable conclusions using as few comparisons as possible. In this paper, we present Vector-Borda Empirical-Gap Elimination (VB-EGE), a fixed-confidence adaptive sampling algorithm for efficiently identifying models on the Pareto frontier in arena-style evaluation, where each comparison evaluates a pair of models on a prompt with respect to a selected performance dimension. VB-EGE progressively eliminates models from an active set once sufficient statistical evidence has been accumulated to certify their Pareto status. Under a multi-objective Bradley-Terry model, we show that VB-EGE returns the correct Pareto frontier with high probability and derive an instance-dependent upper bound on its sample complexity. We further establish a worst-case lower bound showing that VB-EGE is minimax-optimal up to logarithmic factors. Simulations and experiments on three real-world Arena datasets (Arena, SearchArena, and VisionArena) demonstrate VB-EGE's empirical effectiveness.

title: Central Limit Theorems for Optimal Transport Functionals
summary: We establish central limit theorems for empirical plug-in estimators of scalar functionals of quadratic optimal transport maps and potentials, including Wasserstein costs and several risk measures constructed from transport-based multivariate quantiles. We study the one-sample problem with a known reference distribution and i.i.d. observations from the target distribution. A natural approach is to combine a limit theorem for the empirical transport map with the functional delta method. We show, however, that in dimensions at least two, empirical transport-map errors admit no nonzero weak limit in $L^2$ under any normalizing scale. Instead, we linearize the functional directly in the target distribution, obtaining an influence-function expansion with a remainder controlled by the transport-map error. The influence function is characterized by a linear elliptic partial differential equation. Under regularity conditions, we use this expansion to prove central limit theorems in low dimensions and establish validity of the empirical bootstrap. We also derive semiparametric efficiency bounds and show that the plug-in estimators attain them under the same conditions.

title: Practical Advantages of Online Conformal Prediction for Data Streams
summary: Full conformal prediction offers finite-sample marginal coverage guarantees under exchangeability, but exact computation can be costly, while its classical guarantees do not directly extend to non-stationary data streams. We compare four sequential conformal regression procedures with a weighted full-conformal benchmark in terms of empirical coverage, prediction interval width, and computational cost. The procedures combine ordinary or forgetting-factor least squares with uniform or exponentially weighted empirical residual quantiles, or with online gradient-based quantile tracking. Experiments cover an independent and identically distributed control, two synthetic distribution-shift scenarios, and four real-world data streams. Adapting the regression model as well as the conformal threshold substantially improves the coverage--width tradeoff under drift. The quantile-tracking procedure requires $O(p^2)$ time and memory per observation, independently of stream length, although its coverage can deteriorate after abrupt changes. These results illustrate the practical tradeoffs between predictor adaptation, uncertainty quantification, and computational resources.

title: Composite Variable Strategies for Continuous Endpoints
summary: Composite endpoints are common in clinical trials for binary, time-to-event or recurrent outcomes. Recently, there has been interest in estimands for continuous endpoints that employ a composite variable strategy for handling intercurrent events, whereby a value on the continuous scale is defined as the outcome. In this paper we describe these continuous composite endpoints where participants who experience the intercurrent event are assigned a pre-specified value on the outcome scale (which we call the failure value) instead of a measurement. We describe these endpoints and the difficulty of choosing the failure value when the mean is the chosen summary statistic. The large impact of the choice of failure value on the variance of the distribution of the endpoint is quantified as a function of the probability of the event and the standardised difference of the failure value from the mean of the unaffected values. Strategies for choosing failure values are discussed, emphasising the need to balance the clinical relevance and interpretability of the estimand with the need to reliably estimate it. Two potential solutions to situations where there is no relevant and viable choice of failure value are proposed; using failure values based on distributional characteristics to generate clinical relevance and using alternative summary measures to avoid the need to select specific values.

title: Inference for Directions in Canonical Correlation Analysis with Partially Paired Data
summary: Canonical correlation analysis (CCA) is a classical tool for learning linear associations between two data views, and inference on canonical directions is the key for interpreting their coefficients and detecting interesting relationships. We study the problem of hypothesis testing for canonical directions when paired observations are supplemented by unpaired observations of either view. The key challenge is to incorporate the additional marginal information while accounting for its dependence on the paired sample used to estimate the canonical directions. To address this issue, we propose coupled augmentation functions that jointly use the marginal information from both views and construct a one-step estimator based on the resulting corrections. Theoretically, we show that under the null, the proposed estimator is consistent and asymptotically normal even when dimension grows at the rate $d = o(n)$. This result provides a sign-invariant Wald test statistic for detecting important variables in canonical directions. Through numerical studies, we show that the proposed test statistic with semi-paired data improves upon inference using paired data.

title: What Moved the Alarm Score? Causal Attribution with Exact Computation and Scarce-Incident Estimation
summary: Alarms in industrial systems and scientific instruments often demand immediate diagnosis despite scarce incident data. To guide intervention, an explanation must trace how changes in the data-generating process propagate through the causal structure to alter the alarm score, rather than merely flagging shifts that may be downstream effects. Treating structural functions and exogenous laws as distinct players yields a finer-grained, function/law-resolved report of how each type of change propagates to the alarm score. title: Optimal aggregation in multiclass classification
summary:

title: Efficient Bayesian Filtering and Inference for Integro-Difference Equation Models
comment: 19 pages, 6 figures, 3 tables; supplementary material (11 pages, 21 figures, 8 tables); accompanying Python package at the repository https://gitlab.com/tatephughes/JAX-IDEM
summary:
Integro-Difference Equation (IDE) models are a class of dynamic spatio-temporal models which describe the temporal evolution of a spatial process, usually to model advection and diffusion of some random field over time.
  While several papers have focused on inference and performance of these models, little attention has been given to computational comparisons of various methods of computing posterior densities and performing inference.
  We address this problem in two parts.
  Firstly, in inference for these models, Kalman filtering (and smoothing) is often used; either to compute marginal likelihoods, or to sample from the hidden process conditional on the rest of the parameters of the model.
  There are many variations of the Kalman filter and smoother with substantially varying performance profiles and stability: the standard Kalman filter, its square-root form, its information form, to name a few.
  The information filters, when set up correctly, can compute the likelihood in $\mathcal O(nr^2 + r^3)$ time per time point ($n$ being the number of observations per time point), where the computation in $n$ can be done in parallel, on models with independent observation error.
  In this paper, we analyse these forms in the context of IDEs, considering computational speed and stability.
  Secondly, there are two main methods of inference used for the kind of dynamical system that IDEs can be reduced to; directly using the marginal likelihood without the hidden state, or constructing a block Gibbs sampler with the hidden state.
  We compare these two approaches in terms of computational efficiency and practical performance in the IDE setting.
  Using a block Gibbs sampler for inference on the system parameters proves to be more efficient in most cases, with a specific real-data example providing an exception.

title: A plug-in estimator of the non-iterative conditional expectation g-formula using long short-term memory models
summary: The non-iterative conditional expectation (NICE) plug-in estimator of the g-formula can be used to estimate the causal effects of sustained treatment strategies, even in the presence of treatment-confounder feedback, under the assumptions of exchangeability, positivity, and consistency. title: Bayesian Neural Networks via Dirichlet Process Priors on the Data-Generating Distribution for Randomized Value Functions in Deep Reinforcement Learning

title: Discrete Exterior Calculus-based Whittle-Matérn Fields on Meshes
summary: This work presents a sparse precision formulation for Whittle-Matérn fields based on Discrete Exterior Calculus. By treating the $k$-cochain as the latent object to be modeled, we show that a single formulation can produce Whittle-Matérn fields for all $k$ and integer $α$ values. By utilising Whitney maps we can enable a push-forward of the prior on 1-cochains, enabling inference for discrete vector fields. We demonstrate this model on interpolation of vector fields on a sphere.

title: Positive, monotone, and convex Gaussian process regression with Laplacian eigenfunctions
summary: We study how to condition an existing Hilbert space Gaussian process (HSGP) expansion on positivity, monotonicity, or convexity throughout an interval. The expansion has Gaussian coefficients whose variances are given by the kernel's spectral density. At fixed covariance and noise parameters, we retain this coefficient law and represent each complete interval event as a threshold on one coefficient. Integrating out that coefficient gives a strongly log-concave marginal posterior with a normal survival weight, while conditional truncated normal sampling recovers the full constrained law. The construction also covers joint restrictions within the finite expansion. For individual restrictions, we characterize the thresholds through polynomial equations and bound posterior error from conservative numerical evaluation in total variation. Under spectral regularity, the conditioned finite posteriors converge in quadratic Wasserstein distance to the corresponding conditioned underlying GP posteriors as the computational interval expands and higher frequencies are retained. This convergence controls uniform discrepancies in the response and derivatives through the constrained order. title: Structural equation modelling--based meta-analytic model for diagnostic test accuracy studies
summary: Bivariate random-effects models are commonly used to jointly synthesize sensitivity and specificity in diagnostic test accuracy (DTA) meta-analysis. title: Doubly Robust Estimation and Inference for Longitudinal Win Probabilities with Ordinal Outcomes in Observational Studies
summary: Repeated ordinal outcomes capture how treatment benefits and harms evolve over time. title: Ask to Learn: Query-Based Collaborative Reinforcement Learning
summary: Offline reinforcement learning is fundamentally limited by the coverage of the available data, while collecting additional trajectories through online exploration may be costly, unsafe, or infeasible. We study whether this limitation can be overcome without directly interacting with the underlying environment. Motivated by practical settings such as collaborator-mediated simulation, where a collaborator can provide information complementary to the offline data, we introduce query-based collaborative reinforcement learning to study how to acquire this information efficiently. The learner starts with a fixed offline dataset and adaptively queries state-time pairs; the collaborator samples an action according to a fixed, possibly suboptimal policy, and the simulator returns the corresponding reward and next state. For finite-horizon tabular problems, we derive an instance-dependent information-theoretic lower bound on the additional queries required to identify an $ε$-optimal policy and develop a local quadratic approximation. Guided by this characterization, we develop an adaptive query-allocation algorithm whose query complexity nearly matches the local benchmark under suitable conditions. Experiments on multiple synthetic and semi-synthetic environments demonstrate the empirical efficiency of the proposed method.

title: Gaussian Approximation of Besov Functions for Logistic Classification on Manifolds
summary: We study Gaussian kernel approximation and regularized logistic classification on a connected compact smooth embedded manifold $X\subset\mathbb R^d$ without boundary and of intrinsic dimension $\varrho$. The performance of the proposed method is evaluated through a simulation study. An application to the Breast Cancer Family Registry data highlights the ability of the model to provide personalized estimation of the risk of developing breast cancer or ovarian cancer as the first event within the competing risks framework.

title: Annealed correlation and quenched noise sensitivity in biased deep neural networks
summary: In earlier work by Jonasson, Steif and Zetterqvist (2023), fully connected deep neural networks with layers of width $n$, i.i.d.\ standard Gaussian weights, sign activations and no bias terms were shown to be annealed and quenched noise sensitive with respect to any joint probability distribution $\mathbb{Q}^{(n)}$ on the input $\boldsymbolω$ and its perturbation $\boldsymbolη$ satisfying a mild positive-correlation condition and $\mathbb{Q}^{(n)}(\boldsymbolη \in \{\boldsymbolω,-\boldsymbolω\}) \to 0$. Here we add independent Gaussian biases of the natural order and show that quenched noise sensitivity is retained over a broad range of depths, indeed under the slightly weaker assumption that $\mathbb{Q}^{(n)}(\boldsymbolω = \boldsymbolη) \to 0$. Thus, subject to the positive-correlation condition, quenched noise sensitivity holds under the minimal requirement that the perturbed input is asymptotically unlikely to coincide with the original input. At the same time, the annealed covariance remains bounded away from zero and is entirely accounted for by fluctuations in the network-dependent output means.

summary: A classical approach for importance sampling (IS) of a rare event is to tilt the measure using its large deviation minimizer, thereby shifting the proposal mean towards the event set. Our analysis addresses both the coefficient of variation of the different proposals and their necessary and sufficient sample size based on the Kullback--Leibler divergence of the IS target from the proposal; both yield the same rates in $\varepsilon$. We demonstrate the resulting samplers, including a variant that blends the classical and the new proposal across noise levels, for a stochastic Korteweg--de Vries equation with thousands of random inputs.

In this paper, we present Vector-Borda Empirical-Gap Elimination (VB-EGE), a fixed-confidence adaptive sampling algorithm for efficiently identifying models on the Pareto frontier in arena-style evaluation, where each comparison evaluates a pair of models on a prompt with respect to a selected performance dimension. VB-EGE progressively eliminates models from an active set once sufficient statistical evidence has been accumulated to certify their Pareto status. Under a multi-objective Bradley-Terry model, we show that VB-EGE returns the correct Pareto frontier with high probability and derive an instance-dependent upper bound on its sample complexity. We further establish a worst-case lower bound showing that VB-EGE is minimax-optimal up to logarithmic factors. Simulations and experiments on three real-world Arena datasets (Arena, SearchArena, and VisionArena) demonstrate VB-EGE's empirical effectiveness.

summary: Gaussian process upper confidence bound (GP-UCB) has been widely studied, though its known regret upper bound is suboptimal. To obtain near-optimal regret upper bounds, existing studies mainly focus on non-adaptive methods, such as uncertainty sampling, whose practical effectiveness is often limited. This paper shows that, under a Gaussian noise assumption, UCB-style algorithms can achieve near-optimal regret upper bounds via data thinning, a statistical technique for creating independent datasets from a single dataset. First, we show that data thinning can yield tighter confidence intervals in the bandit setting, and that a direct extension of GP-UCB achieves a near-optimal simple regret upper bound. Furthermore, by leveraging the tighter confidence intervals and combining GP-UCB with a phased elimination algorithm, we show a near-optimal cumulative regret upper bound. Finally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of UCB-style algorithms incorporating data thinning via numerical experiments.

This component is derived from the known asymptotic approximation to the optimal zero-variance proposal distribution. The second mixture component is designed to cover missing event mass due to boundary-approximation mismatch, thereby preserving unbiasedness. We rigorously analyze this sampling strategy's performance as a function of event geometry, dimension, rarity level, and number $N$ of importance samples. Under explicit and relatively mild conditions on the former three features, we prove that the squared relative error of GeoIS is bounded by $c/N$ with high probability, for an absolute constant $c$. We implement our method numerically in several examples, including a diffusion PDE problem. The numerical experiments exhibit the qualitative dependence on geometry, dimension, rarity and sample size predicted by the theory, and show that GeoIS markedly outperforms importance sampling methods that use a fully Gaussian proposal distribution.

title: Divide-and-Conquer Neural Bayes Estimation for Spatial and Spatiotemporal Point Process Models

title: Mixture of Censored Partially Linear Experts Models for Symmetric or Asymmetric Data with or without Outlying Observations: A novel approach with two-piece scale-mixture of normal distributions

title: Predicting silent failures of learned inference under restricted access: what measurement physics and prior information explain

summary: Learned priors are used to reconstruct regions that measurements barely reach, and to report uncertainty there. title: Nonparametric In-Context Learning and Inference via Measure-Indexed Kernel Ridge Regression
summary: In-Context learning enables an estimator, trained across multiple tasks, to adapt to a new unseen task solely through its in-context samples, without any parameter refitting. We further prove that the proposed estimator is pointwise asymptotically normal, enabling the construction of confidence intervals for the mean and prediction intervals for the response on an unseen task. Notably, the estimator achieves valid uncertainty quantification without any refitting when adapting to a new task. As a special case, our framework recovers classical distributed nonparametric regression when all tasks share the same underlying function. The proposed framework is illustrated through a latent Gaussian process example.

title: Control variates for dry friction under colored noise: variance rates for non-smooth observables
summary:

For smooth observables, the asymptotic variance is $O(\varepsilon^{2})$, where $\varepsilon^{2}$ is the correlation time of the noise. However, for non-smooth reliability observables, such as threshold indicators and overshoot severities, rate estimates have not been established in general.

The last three bounds hold up to logarithmic factors. Bounds on the bias of the white-noise approximation and non-asymptotic sample-size estimates are also derived, and the comparison principle is shown to be preserved under coupled time discretization. Numerical experiments in the three regimes support the predicted rates.

title: A general class of shared gamma frailty models for risk prediction, with application to breast cancer screening adherence
summary: We introduce a new class of mixed models for longitudinal or clustered binary data. We focus on an easily interpretable specification of the model, discuss the associated individual risk prediction, and compare our results to the traditional GLMM model for binary data with random intercept. Overall, our approach provides a flexible Bayesian estimation of direct and spillover effect decomposition in the presence of treatment noncompliance.

title: Geometry-Aware Block Selection for Sparse Variational Gaussian Processes
summary: Sparse variational Gaussian processes (SVGPs) are a widely used, principled approach to scalable Gaussian process modelling. Their success stems from their theoretically interpretable structure: they provide a lower bound on the marginal likelihood of the full GP while allowing scal- able stochastic optimization. Recent work has explored modifications of the posterior conditional distribution and has shown that such extensions can improve upon this well-established framework. In particular, introducing a block-diagonal structured scal- ing matrix leads to a tighter lower bound on the GP marginal likelihood. Since the scaling matrix contributes to the variational lower bound through an upper bound on the log-determinant of the full residual covariance matrix, our work makes the following contributions. First, we introduce a simple, scalable, geometry-aware algorithm, with explicit computational complexity and low computational overhead, that recovers a large fraction of this log- determinant contribution by selecting an appropriate partition of the data. Second, we show how to train these models using a doubly stochastic optimization framework. title: Likelihood-Based Confidence Curves for Bounded Parameters
summary: When a parameter is bounded, the likelihood ratio statistic does not generally follow the chi-square limit distribution of Wilks' theorem. In fact, its asymptotic null distribution depends on the distance from the null value to the boundary, interpolating between the chi-bar-square law on the boundary and the chi-square law in the deep interior of the parameter space. We derive this distribution and use it to construct confidence curves, which are nested collections of two-sided confidence intervals or regions, for bounded parameters. We extend the existing result for the scalar parameter to a two-dimensional parameter with one or both components bounded. As the bivariate distributions are integrals of normal distributions, which are not reducible to standard statistical functions, we also give a simpler approximated distribution obtained by moment-matching. We illustrate the methods on a canonical analysis from high-energy physics, namely the Poisson signal-plus-background experiment.

summary: Confirmatory trials increasingly test several treatments against a common control, and many balance prognostic factors through covariate-adaptive randomization (CAR). For time-to-event endpoints, they usually rely on the stratified log-rank test and the hazard ratio, but the former may lose power and the latter its clear interpretation when hazards are not proportional. The restricted mean survival time (RMST) provides an interpretable alternative, yet inference for multiple RMST comparisons under CAR remains largely unexplored. Under Pocock--Simon minimization, their limiting covariance contains a design term that arises only when the randomization factors interact in their effect on survival. We then develop test statistics that account for the shared control and the randomization design. Calibrated by a Gaussian multiplier, the resulting max-$T$ procedures control the family-wise error rate and give simultaneous confidence bands over restriction times. In simulations, the method controls the Type I error rate under various randomization procedures and outperforms the stratified log-rank test when the benefit wanes. An application based on the three-arm ICON6 trial illustrates its practicality.

title: Debiased Prior-Data Fitted Networks for Amortized Bayesian Semi-Parametric Inference
summary: Prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) have recently gained popularity as an end-to-end approach to amortized Bayesian inference. First, we show that, despite being Bayes-optimal with respect to the target, an idealized PFN can exhibit a posterior concentration rate that implicitly depends on the concentration rates of (latent) nuisance functions and can become slower as the prior becomes more diverse. Then, to speed up the target posterior concentration rates, we introduce two generic debiasing strategies based on efficient influence functions: (i) a label correction and (ii) a prior correction. Finally, we show that the debiased PFNs (i) & (ii) possess concentration rates that asymptotically match a convergence rate given by traditional frequentist bias-corrected estimators. In this way, we establish a novel connection between amortized Bayesian inference with PFNs and frequentist semi-parametric efficiency theory. Therefore, our work provides guidelines for designing debiased PFNs for semi-parametric inference with principled and provable asymptotic guarantees.

title: Confessions of a Masked MDP
summary:
In reinforcement learning, one presumes the action set to be known ahead of time, and, thus, one must know if any state-action pairs are not permissible
  ahead of computations. In some applications, determining this action mask is the main computational bottleneck. Isolating this problem to highlight its core
  properties, we study how to combine the search for an optimal policy with the learning of the mask itself, under a linear MDP model in which each attempted
  action reveals the exact value of a linear score determining its validity. In this framework, we first construct an algorithm based on deterministic
  optimistic optimization and show that it is minimax optimal, which we show is also computationally efficient. However, it is sub-optimal on non-degenerate
  instances, as we show. We propose an alternative, which is also computationally efficient, which plans its exploration strategy. This algorithm admits a
  formal interpretation as an analogue of information-directed-sampling for deterministic feedback, which may be of independent interest. Finally, we study an
  application of this framework to transfer learning, where the invalid action set changes over time.

title: Functional meta-analysis of survival curves across reporting formats and time points
summary: Meta-analyses of survival outcomes commonly pool log hazard ratios or survival probabilities at selected time points. When reporting formats and observation times differ across studies, methods are needed to use available survival information for estimation at a common target time. We propose a functional random-effects model on the complementary log--log scale that synthesizes Kaplan--Meier curves and survival probabilities at discrete times as functional data. Studies that do not report survival at the target time contribute to its estimation through the use of their observed curves to estimate group-specific mean functions. The estimated between-group contrast is interpreted as a log hazard ratio under proportional hazards and as a time-specific log cumulative hazard ratio under non-proportional hazards. In simulations with delayed effects and crossing survival curves, the root mean squared error for the log cumulative hazard ratio was lower than that of the two-stage Cox method, and interval coverage was close to the nominal level. In an application to disease-free survival in resectable non-small cell lung cancer, the two-stage Cox method estimated an average hazard ratio, whereas the proposed method captured nonlinear changes in the cumulative hazard ratio over time.

A key benefit of this principled modularization is that it greatly simplifies inference, reducing a fully joint mixture analysis to sampling label allocations, fitting the protected downstream model for each sample, and averaging the resulting posteriors. For Mahalanobis distance-based rerandomization, we derive the asymptotic distributions of the Horvitz-Thompson and Hájek estimators under approximate neighborhood interference and quantify the resulting precision gains. At the analysis stage, we propose a covariate adjustment method that acts directly on these estimation errors. This method requires no normalization of the auxiliary variables and is optimal within the corresponding class of linear adjustments. We show that rerandomization and covariate adjustment become asymptotically equivalent as the rerandomization threshold approaches zero, extending this equivalence to settings with interference. For high-dimensional auxiliary variables, we propose Lasso-adjusted estimators and establish their joint asymptotic normality under suitable sparsity conditions. These estimators retain the same asymptotic distribution when combined with fixed-dimensional rerandomization. Simulations and a social-network application illustrate the precision gains from the proposed methods.

title: On the Accuracy of Approximate Leave-One-Out with Blockwise Nonsmooth Regularization in High-dimensions
summary:

These methods have recently attracted increased attention because of their connections to other important problems, including machine unlearning and data valuation. For empirical risk minimization, ALO methods often rely on a few Newton steps and therefore require smooth loss functions and regularizers. In high-dimensional problems, however, regularizers are frequently non-smooth. This has motivated the development of heuristic ALO methods for non-smooth regularization, whose empirical accuracy is often strong but whose theoretical justification remains limited.
  In this paper, we study the accuracy of a heuristic ALO method for a broad class of non-differentiable penalties that promote block sparsity in the proportional high-dimensional regime. Assuming uniformly bounded block sizes, we prove that the expected average absolute discrepancy between the exact leave-one-out loss and its ALO approximation is $O(\log^{3/2}(en)/\sqrt{n})$. Our proof technique differs substantially from existing approaches and relies on obtaining sharp bounds on the number of active groups whose status changes between the full-data and leave-one-out estimators. In addition to yielding stronger guarantees under weaker assumptions than prior work, our analysis provides new insight into the stability of sparse estimators under perturbations of the training data.

title: Variance estimation for generalized linear regression with binary outcome when using case-cohort data
summary: The case-cohort design was initially proposed for studying rare outcomes in large cohorts, where covariates may be too expensive to measure on all the subjects. Because of its sampling scheme, this design often requires intricate variance estimation. However, there is significantly less publications on the use of case-cohort data with binary outcomes than for case-cohort survival analysis, notably regarding inference. In this work, an influence-based variance estimation method is proposed for parameters obtained from log-linear or logistic regression models and case-cohort data. The approach is flexible and is illustrated on two cohort subsampling designs: (i) a design possibly stratified on some correlate of the covariates but where sampling of the cases is exhaustive; (ii) a design where the sampling is further stratified based on case status. The variance estimation method properly accounts for the sampling features and allows appropriate analysis of case-cohort data. It is illustrated on a simulation and on data from the National Wilms Tumor Study Group. Influences, and therefore variance estimates, can be easily computed from outputs of standard R commands such as glm and glmgee. In addition to being much less computationally intensive, influence-based variance estimation is more reliable than bootstrap variance estimation, recently proposed by Noma [Journal of Epidemiology, 2024].
